paras: The Setauket rubber factory riot was an attack in late October or early November 1882 by Irish and other white residents of Setauket, Long Island, New York, on the town's Black residents, who, like the Irish, had recently come there in large numbers to work in the rubber factory. After a white man was reported beaten by Black men, whites beat every Black man they found on the streets and attacked Black homes until armed Black residents drove them off. No deaths were reported, and the story ran nationally as a race feud under headings such as "An Irish-African Feud" and "A War of Races."

According to a New York dispatch of November 4, a feud had broken out at Setauket between "colored and Irish people" who had recently arrived "in great numbers" to work in the rubber factory. A few nights before the dispatch, a white man was badly beaten; the wire said "some negroes" did it, one condensed version said "a negro," and the New-York Tribune said "several negroes." The Tribune named the man as John Muller and reported that his jaw bone was broken.

In retaliation, whites beat every Black man they found on the street, using stones and clubs, and several persons were badly injured. The Tribune described the attackers as the injured man's friends, who "sought satisfaction" by attacking every colored man they met. The attackers then went to the Black residents' dwellings and broke windows and doors.

The Black residents finally appeared armed with shotguns, and their assailants fled. A rewritten version in weekly news summaries said the fight "became general" and that the attackers set fire to the Black quarters before fire-arms drove them off. Dispatches closed by saying that further trouble was feared, and a brief item the following week reported trouble still "pending" between Irish and colored laborers at the rubber works.

A later news summary in the Perrysburg Journal of Ohio gave further names: Samuel Smith, colored, was "terribly clubbed," and Stephen Johnson cut two men and a woman with a razor. No report of arrests, charges or court proceedings appears in the coverage.

The story reached most readers through the New York wire of November 4, printed on November 5 in papers from St. Paul and Memphis to Seattle, Omaha, Miles City and Las Vegas, New Mexico, and later in Bismarck. Editors framed it as an ethnic contest, with headlines such as "An Irish-African Feud," "Ethiopia vs. Ireland," "Fighting Factions," "A War of Races" and "A Desperate State of Things." Several papers garbled the town's name as "Selauket," "Setanket," "Selanket," "Senaket" or "Zeanket."

Closer to home, the New-York Tribune ran the item in its Long Island column among other local news, adding the white victim's name and his injury. Later summaries reshaped the account: the Grenada Sentinel's version added the burning of the Black quarters, while the Perrysburg Journal treated the affair as a fight between "rival operators" in the factory over "a fancied injury."

The accounts differ on the date: the wire placed the first beating a few nights before November 4, while the Perrysburg Journal dated a fight to the night of November 9, after the wire was sent. Because the later summary repeats Muller's broken jaw, it may describe the same clash with a wrong date rather than a second outbreak. Only the summary version reported that the Black quarters were set on fire; the wire and the Tribune mentioned broken windows and doors but no fire.

bases: After a white man was beaten, whites beat 'every colored man' found on the streets and attacked the Black residents' dwellings, a collective attack on the town's Black newcomers (A1, A8, A17).

The New York wire (A1, A2, A15), the New-York Tribune's local column with a name and injury not in the wire (A8), and a later news summary with further names (A20) agree on a clash between Black and Irish rubber-factory workers with beatings and injuries, though they differ on date and details.

framing.detail: Western papers ran the New York wire under headings such as 'An Irish-African Feud', 'A War of Races' and 'A Desperate State of Things', presenting it as a race feud with further trouble feared.
The New-York Tribune carried it as a short local item, naming the white victim and saying his friends 'sought satisfaction'.
The Perrysburg Journal's summary treated it as a fight between rival factory operators caused by 'a fancied injury'.

conflicts.note: The Nov. 9 date falls after the wire was sent; it may be a second clash or a misdated summary of the same one, since the same names (Muller, jaw broken) recur.
